The Bridled parrotfish (Scarus frenatus) is a herbivorous scarid found on coral reefs throughout the Indo-Pacific, where its beak-like fused teeth allow it to graze algae directly from the reef substrate. Newly hatched larvae are minute, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00015 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00015 grams], a value derived from the egg diameter of the related parrotfish Calotomus japonicus, reflecting the small, pelagic eggs typical of broadcast-spawning scarids. This tiny starting mass necessitates rapid early growth to escape the size window of highest vulnerability to planktivorous predators.

Juvenile Bridled parrotfish grow rapidly on the reef, transitioning through a series of color phases before reaching sexual maturity. Individuals reach the total length at puberty of 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters], at which point the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 171.5 grams [Wwp = approximately 171.5 grams]. This substantial early growth reflects the abundant algal resources available on healthy reef flats, which support rapid somatic development during the juvenile phase.

Adults of this species ultimately attain a total length of 47 centimeters [Li = 47 centimeters], with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of approximately 2,400 grams [Wwi = approximately 2,400 grams]. This substantial adult body size supports the species' role as a major bioeroder on coral reefs, as its continuous grazing and excavation of the reef substrate contributes significantly to the production of fine carbonate sediment.

Reproductive condition in the Bridled parrotfish is closely tied to gonadal development. Under a water temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches approximately 4% [GSI = approximately 4%], a value estimated from data on the related parrotfish Hipposcarus longiceps. Longevity in this species reaches a maximum of approximately 20 years [am = approximately 20 years] at the same reference temperature, a considerable lifespan for a reef fish of this size and one that reflects the relatively low natural mortality experienced by adults occupying stable, resource-rich coral reef habitats at a temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C].
